subject: Engineering Mathematics
summary: matrix algebra, rank, systems of linear equations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors

questions.text:
The rank of the matrix
123
246
111
is
solution: Concept: Rank = number of non-zero rows after row reduction = order of the largest non-zero minor.
R<sub>2</sub> = 2R<sub>1</sub>, so R<sub>2</sub> → R<sub>2</sub> − 2R<sub>1</sub> gives a zero row. det A = 0, so rank < 3.
R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> are not proportional: the minor |1 2; 1 1| = 1 − 2 = −1 ≠ 0.
Rank = 2
Exam tip: Look for proportional rows or columns first; it often settles the rank without full elimination.

questions.text:
The determinant of
213
045
106
is ______
solution: Concept: Expand along a row or column with zeros to save work.
Exam tip: Watch the sign pattern + − + along the first row; the middle term flips sign.

questions.text: The system x + y + z = 6, x + 2y + 3z = 10, x + 2y + λz = μ has no solution when
solution: Concept: Compare rank(A) with rank of the augmented matrix [A | b]. Unequal ranks → no solution.
R<sub>3</sub> − R<sub>2</sub> gives (0, 0, λ − 3 | μ − 10).
λ ≠ 3: rank A = 3 = rank [A|b] → unique solution.
λ = 3, μ = 10: both ranks 2 → infinitely many solutions.
λ = 3, μ ≠ 10: rank A = 2, rank [A|b] = 3 → no solution.
Exam tip: Reduce only the row that contains λ and μ; the other rows need no work.

questions.text:
For A =
200
130
456
, the trace of A³ is ______
solution: Concept: If λ is an eigenvalue of A then λ³ is an eigenvalue of A³, and trace = sum of eigenvalues.
A is lower triangular, so its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries 2, 3, 6.
Eigenvalues of A³: 8, 27, 216
Exam tip: Never multiply out A³ in the exam. Triangular → read eigenvalues from the diagonal.

questions.text:
An eigenvector of
21
12
corresponding to the eigenvalue 3 is
solution: Concept: Solve (A − λI)x = 0 for λ = 3.
Eigenvector: [1, 1]ᵀ (any non-zero multiple).
Check: A[1, 1]ᵀ = [3, 3]ᵀ = 3[1, 1]ᵀ ✓. [1, −1]ᵀ belongs to λ = 1.
Exam tip: In an MCQ, just multiply each option by A and see which comes out as λ times itself.

questions.text:
For A =
12
34
, A⁴ can be written as pA + qI. The value of p is ______
solution: Concept: Cayley–Hamilton: every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.
Characteristic equation: λ² − (trace)λ + det = λ² − 5λ − 2 = 0 → A² = 5A + 2I
Exam tip: Cayley–Hamilton also gives the inverse: A⁻¹ = (A − 5I)/2 here.

questions.text: Which statement about a real symmetric matrix is NOT always true?
opts: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal
It can be diagonalised by an orthogonal matrix
solution: Concept: The spectral theorem guarantees real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors and orthogonal diagonalisation for every real symmetric matrix.
Invertibility needs every eigenvalue to be non-zero, which is not guaranteed.

Counter-example:
11
11
is symmetric but det = 0 (eigenvalues 0 and 2).
So 'It is invertible' is the false statement.
Exam tip: Symmetric says nothing about singularity; a zero eigenvalue is allowed.

questions.text: A is a 4 × 5 real matrix of rank 3. The number of linearly independent solutions of Ax = 0 is ______
solution: Concept: Rank–nullity theorem: rank + nullity = number of unknowns (columns).
Unknowns n = 5, rank r = 3
Nullity = n − r = 5 − 3 = 2
Exam tip: Use the number of columns, not rows. 4 − 3 = 1 is the usual slip.

questions.text:
If A =
12
21
, the eigenvalues of A² + 2A + I are
solution: Concept: If Ax = λx then f(A)x = f(λ)x for any polynomial f.
Eigenvalues of A: λ² − 2λ − 3 = 0 → λ = 3, −1
Eigenvalues of A² + 2A + I: 16 and 0
Exam tip: Note that A² + 2A + I is singular here, because one of its eigenvalues is zero.

questions.text: A 3 × 3 matrix A has eigenvalues 1, 2 and 3. The determinant of adj(A) is ______
solution: Concept: det(adj A) = (det A)n−1 for an n × n matrix.
det A = product of eigenvalues = 1 × 2 × 3 = 6
det(adj A) = 63−1 = 6² = 36
Exam tip: Also remember adj(adj A) = (det A)n−2 A.

questions.text: Solving 2x + y − z = 1, x + 3y + 2z = 13, 3x − y + 4z = 13 by Gauss elimination, the value of z is
solution: Concept: Eliminate x, then y, then back-substitute.
R<sub>2</sub> → 2R<sub>2</sub> − R<sub>1</sub>: 5y + 5z = 25 → y + z = 5
R<sub>3</sub> → 2R<sub>3</sub> − 3R<sub>1</sub>: −5y + 11z = 23
Adding 5(y + z = 5): 16z = 48 → z = 3, then y = 2 and x = 1.
Exam tip: Substitute (1, 2, 3) back into all three equations. It takes 10 seconds and catches sign errors.

questions.text:
The rank of
1234
2468
3579
1111
is ______
solution: Concept: Rank = number of linearly independent rows.
R<sub>2</sub> = 2R<sub>1</sub>, so R<sub>2</sub> adds nothing.
R<sub>3</sub> = 2R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>4</sub>: 2[1, 2, 3, 4] + [1, 1, 1, 1] = [3, 5, 7, 9] ✓, so R<sub>3</sub> adds nothing either.
R1 and R4 are not proportional → rank = 2
Exam tip: Rows whose entries are in arithmetic progression (1 2 3 4, 3 5 7 9, 1 1 1 1) always give rank ≤ 2.

questions.text: The system kx + y = 0, x + ky = 0 has a non-trivial solution when
solution: Concept: A homogeneous system has non-trivial solutions only if the coefficient matrix is singular.
Check k = 1: x + y = 0 twice → x = −y, infinitely many solutions ✓
Exam tip: Homogeneous systems are always consistent; the only question is whether det = 0.

questions.text:
The largest eigenvalue of
311
131
113
is ______
solution: Concept: A = 2I + J, where J is the all-ones matrix. J has eigenvalues 3, 0, 0.
So A has eigenvalues 2 + 3 = 5, 2 + 0 = 2, 2 + 0 = 2.
Largest = 5. Check: trace = 9 = 5 + 2 + 2 ✓; det = 20 = 5 × 2 × 2 ✓
Exam tip: Equal row sums s mean s is an eigenvalue with eigenvector [1, 1, 1]ᵀ. Here every row sums to 5.

questions.text:
The matrix
11
01
has
solution: Concept: Number of independent eigenvectors for λ = n − rank(A − λI) (geometric multiplicity).
Eigenvalue λ = 1 is repeated (algebraic multiplicity 2).
A − I = [0 1; 0 0] has rank 1 → independent eigenvectors = 2 − 1 = 1 (only [1, 0]ᵀ).
So A is not diagonalisable.
Exam tip: A repeated eigenvalue does not guarantee a full set of eigenvectors; check the rank of A − λI.
